1.2: Warm to outsiders, impatient with your parents: what is missing?
1.3: Are smooth talkers never to be trusted?
1.4: If you review someone’s plan and only say “looks fine”, is that disloyal?
1.5: Why do the principles of running a state work for a small shop owner too?
1.6: Confucius puts book learning last. Does that mean books can be skipped?
1.7: Why does Zixia say a man who never studied has learned?
1.8: “Have no friends not equal to yourself”: does it really mean avoiding people worse than you?
1.9: Why take more care where no one is watching?
1.10: Every state asked Confucius about government. Did he go looking for it?
1.11: Must a father’s rules be kept for three years even if they are wrong?
1.12: “Harmony is most precious”: does it mean never disagree?
1.13: Why does keeping your word start before you make the promise?
1.14: A gentleman does not eat his fill. Is he starving himself on purpose?
1.15: Poor but not fawning, rich but not showy: why does Confucius only say “not bad”?
1.16: Others not understanding you, or you not understanding others: which matters more?
2.1: The Pole Star stays still. Does that mean officials need do nothing?
2.2: The Odes include love songs and complaints. Why “no swerving thoughts”?
2.3: Fines stop littering. Why is that not enough for Confucius?
2.4: “At thirty I stood firm”: should you stand firm just because you turn thirty?
2.5: Is doing whatever your parents say what filial piety means?
2.6: You stay up late and wear yourself down. Why is that a question of filial piety?
2.7: Sending your parents money every month: how is that different from feeding dogs and horses?
2.8: All the chores are done. What is still missing from filial piety?
2.9: A student who never asks questions: why does Confucius say he is not slow?
2.10: How can you tell when someone is putting on an act?
2.11: “Review the old to know the new”: is it only about revising lessons?
2.12: “A gentleman is not a vessel”: must he be good at everything?
2.13: Say then do, or do then say: what is the difference?
2.14: Two people host the same dinner. Why is one making friends and the other forming a clique?
2.15: Saving hundreds of online lessons you never watch: does that count as learning?
2.16: “Gong hu yiduan”: does it mean attacking heresy?
2.17: Why is saying “I don’t know” a kind of knowing?
2.18: A student asks how to get an official post. What does Confucius say?
2.19: Why can the people tell at once whom you promote?
2.20: Ji Kangzi wants the people obedient. Why does Confucius tell him to govern himself first?
2.21: Confucius held no office. How can he say he too takes part in government?
2.22: Why is a person without good faith like a cart missing its pin?
2.23: Could Confucius really foresee things a hundred generations away?
2.24: Saying nothing in a meeting when you should speak: what would Confucius call it?
3.1: A few extra rows of dancers: why is Confucius so angry?
3.2: They sang an ode reserved for the Son of Heaven. What was wrong with that?
3.3: Someone performs every rite to the letter. Why can rites not save him?
3.4: Lavish rites are wrong and stingy ones too. So what is right?
3.5: “Better without a ruler”: whom is Confucius scolding?
3.6: Your boss wants to break the rules and won’t listen. Do you just let it go?
3.8: A painting needs a white ground first. What about a person?
3.9: Confucius can describe the rites of Xia. Why won’t he make a firm claim?
3.10: The sacrifice is going well. Why does Confucius not want to watch the rest?
3.11: Asked about the di sacrifice, why does Confucius say “I don’t know”?
3.12: Why is a sacrifice done by proxy as good as no sacrifice?
3.13: Praying to the kitchen god works better than the high gods. What does Confucius think?
3.14: Why does Confucius say “I follow Zhou”?
3.15: The man who knows rites best enters the Grand Temple and asks about everything. Why?
3.16: Why is archery not a contest of strength?
3.17: Should one sheep be saved? Why does Confucius argue the point with Zigong?
3.18: Doing things by the book, why is he called a flatterer?
3.19: Ruler and minister: who should do his part first?
3.20: When feeling runs full, how does it keep from going too far?
3.21: “Don’t blame what is past”: does it really mean let it go?
3.22: Why does Confucius call Guan Zhong “small in capacity”?
3.23: What layers does Confucius hear in a fine piece of music?
3.24: How does a minor border official see Confucius’s weight at a glance?
3.25: Two equally beautiful pieces of music: why does Confucius rank them?
3.26: Someone in high place without generosity, at a funeral without grief: why won’t Confucius even look?
4.1: House hunters check schools and transport first. What does Confucius say to check first?
4.2: Why does anyone change after long poverty or long comfort?
4.3: Everyone likes some people and dislikes others. What can the humane do that others can’t?
4.4: Once you set your heart on goodness, can you still go wrong?
4.5: Wealth and rank you haven’t earned arrive at your door. Do you take them?
4.6: Confucius says he has never seen anyone too weak to practise humaneness. Is that true?
4.7: Everyone makes mistakes. How do mistakes show whether a person is humane?
4.8: “Hear the Way in the morning, die content at night”: what is the hard part?
4.9: He says his heart is set on the Way but is ashamed of shabby clothes. What is the problem?
4.10: Why does a gentleman neither commit in advance nor refuse in advance?
4.11: “The petty man cherishes his land”: is it wrong to miss home?
4.12: Why does no one see off the flatmate who only looked after himself?
4.13: The rites are all in order. Why can they still not be put to use?
4.14: No one knows who you are. What should you think about first?
4.15: Confucius’s “one thread through it all”: why does Zengzi call it loyalty and reciprocity?
4.16: Gentleman and petty man both understand clearly. What does each understand?
4.17: Meeting someone better than you, what is your first reaction?
4.18: When parents are in the wrong, how should children speak up?
4.19: “While your parents live, do not travel far”: can we still do that today?
4.20: “Three years without changing the father’s way”: why can’t it stand alone as an iron rule?
4.21: Why does knowing your parents’ age bring both joy and fear?
4.22: Why were the ancients slow to speak?
4.23: Why does holding back make mistakes rare?
4.24: Why does a gentleman say little and do much?
4.25: “Virtue is never alone; it always has neighbours”: does good get rewarded?
4.26: What happens when you advise a friend too often?
5.1: Why did Confucius marry his daughter to a man who had been in prison?
5.2: Why praise a man together with the people around him?
5.3: Confucius calls Zigong “a vessel”. Praise or criticism?
5.4: Why does a quick tongue make people dislike you?
5.5: A student turns down an official post. Why is Confucius pleased?
5.6: Confucius talks of putting out to sea. Why does Zilu take him seriously?
5.7: Why won’t Confucius call his capable students humane?
5.8: Confucius asks Zigong whether he can match Yan Hui. What does he want to hear?
5.9: Zai Wo sleeps in the daytime. Why does Confucius scold him so hard?
5.10: The man who looks the toughest: why does Confucius say he is not firm?
5.11: Zigong says he no longer imposes on others. Why does Confucius say he isn’t there yet?
5.12: Why did Confucius rarely speak of human nature and the Way of Heaven?
5.13: Why was Zilu afraid of hearing something new?
5.14: A man with a poor reputation: how did he earn the posthumous name “Wen”?
5.15: Confucius praises Zichan point by point. What is hidden in the praise?
5.16: Still showing respect after a long friendship: what makes it hard?
5.17: Business is bad, so you redecorate first. What would Confucius say?
5.18: Three times in office, three times out, never showing it. Is that humane?
5.19: “Think three times before acting”: why does Confucius say twice is enough?
5.20: Confucius says Ning Wuzi’s “foolishness” can’t be matched. Foolish in what way?
5.21: In Chen, Confucius cries “Let us go home!” Why stop travelling?
5.22: Bo Yi and Shu Qi were so aloof. Why did few hold grudges against them?
5.23: A neighbour asks for vinegar, so he borrows some to give. Why is that not upright?
5.24: Calling someone a friend while resenting him: why does Confucius find it shameful?
5.25: Confucius and two students each state their aims. How do the three differ?
5.26: Why is knowing you were wrong still not enough?
5.27: In what does Confucius think he outdoes others?
6.1: Keeping things simple: when is it good, and when too simple?
6.2: Why does Confucius’s “love of learning” mean not shifting anger onto others?
6.3: Zihua goes on a mission to Qi. Why does Confucius give his mother only a little grain?
6.4: Can someone from a bad background be employed?
6.5: How does Yan Hui’s humaneness differ from others’?
6.6: Zilu, Zigong, Ran Qiu: which of them could govern?
6.7: Not wanting to serve a powerful minister, how does Min Ziqian turn the post down?
6.8: Visiting a sick student, why does Confucius only hold his hand through the window?
6.9: Yan Hui was so poor. What was he happy about?
6.10: Someone says “I lack the strength.” Is that really so?
6.11: Both read books. What separates the gentleman scholar from the petty scholar?
6.12: He never takes shortcuts or calls at the officer’s door. Why is he worth promoting?
6.13: After a great deed, why does he say his horse was just too slow?
6.14: Without a glib tongue or good looks, in what kind of age is it hard to stay safe?
6.15: Everyone goes out through the door. Why won’t people take the straight road in life?
6.16: Too plain or too polished: which way is better to lean?
6.17: Crooked people live well enough. How to explain that?
6.18: Knowing it, loving it, delighting in it: what is the difference?
6.19: Why does Confucius teach according to who is listening?
6.20: Revering spirits yet keeping them at a distance: belief or not?
